When you press the accelerator in a Tesla, there's no engine to rev, and no cable to pull.
The pedal is just a sensor, telling a computer how far you pressed.
Under the floor, thousands of battery cells hold the energy.
But they give out direct current, and the motor needs alternating current.
So the inverter switches that power on and off thousands of times a second.
It shapes it into three waves of current, one for each set of copper coils in the motor.
Together, they make a magnetic field that spins around inside the motor.
The magnets in the rotor get dragged along, so full force arrives instantly, even from a standstill.
The motor can spin at about eighteen thousand R P M, so a single-speed gearbox slows it down about nine to one.
And when you lift your foot, the motor becomes a generator, and charges the battery.
So pressing the pedal really means one thing: a spinning magnetic field, pulling magnets around.
